newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin faces make or break test in French vote.
newsitem.headline: Jospin faces make or break test in French vote.

text.p: France's parliamentary election offers Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin the possibility of becoming France's next prime minister or a political has-been.

An underdog in the month-long campaign before the two-stage vote on Sunday and June 1, the earnest ex-education minister has revived his battered party as the undisputed main opposition force four years after defeat in a right-wing landslide.

If he wins with his slogan "Let's change the future", Jospin, 59, would realise the Left's dream of returning to power and make conservative President Jacques Chirac the longest-lived political lame duck in French history.
Chirac called the vote 10 months early, hoping his allies would win and rule with him until the end of his term in 2002.

If the Socialists lose, Jospin may be able to bask in the glory of a bigger minority in the 577-seat parliament after winning praise from the grassroots for criss-crossing the country in an energetic campaign.
But it may also call into question his ability to survive.
"In the medium term, I don't think Jospin can stay on as party leader after a failure," said sociologist Alain Touraine.
The tag of "decent loser" that stuck in 1995 when Jospin gained a better-than-expected 47.3 percent of the vote in a runoff for the presidency won by Chirac, may become an epitaph.
During the campaign, opinion polls showed that voters preferred the silver-haired, bespectacled school teacher's son as prime minister to the current incumbent, Alain Juppe.

Tall, lean and intense, Jospin hammered away at Juppe's government over record unemployment and political sleaze, and accused him of secretly preparing a new austerity to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.

However, it seems unlikely he will manage to convert deep disaffection with the centre-right into a groundswell of support for the Socialist programme, which featured pledges to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay.
Friendly and witty in private, Jospin's speeches at campaign rallies often sound as dry and convoluted as the university lectures he used to give.

Some commentators wonder if the Socialists are ready for power -- polls show many people do not yet trust them. "Is Jospin scared of winning?" the magazine L'Evenement du Jeudi asked in a front-page cover.

The popular television puppet satire show "Guignols de L'Info" has portrayed him as "Yoyo", a well-meaning simpleton modelled on Enid Blyton's "Noddy" aimlessly driving round in a toytown car searching for ideas.
Born in 1937 in Meudon, south of Paris, to a family of ardent socialists, he won the nickname "silver tongue" during a brief turn in the boy scouts.
Jospin had a strict Protestant upbringing in an overwhelmingly Roman Catholic country.
Like both Chirac and Juppe, he attended the elite National Administrative College (ENA) -- widely criticised for producing technocratic clones -- and joined the Foreign Ministry.
But frustrated and bored, he dropped out shortly after the 1968 student revolt to become an economics lecturer and joined the Socialist party in 1971.
He describes himself as "warm, straightforward and simple" and says he knows how to have fun, but concedes: "A sense of modesty cramps and confines me a little."
Speaking in his constituency of Cintegabelle near Toulouse, in southwestern France, the Socialist leader said the French people had spoken out very clearly.

The Socialist party and its allies had increased their score substantially from the 1993 parliamentary election and his own result in the 1995 presidential election, Jospin said, while the centre-right had polled its lowest score in many years.
This showed "that the French people seem to see their future on the left", he added.

Calling for a clean debate on issues and proposals instead of insults in the coming week, Jospin said he offered the French people "a pact for change for a new, honest democracy that respects people and listens to them".
